doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Reviewing Hawkins's 'Body and Soul' with 'virgin ears'
summary: Rowe's curveball: how he would review the 1930s Hawkins record; he would find a metaphor, compare influences and consider the rhythm section.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: I’d like to wrap up with — this is sort of a curve ball.

You had mentioned technology and at some point we mentioned 78s. So this is “Body and Soul”/“Foxtrot” Coleman Hawkins and his Orchestra. I wonder if you can imagine, if you were writing reviews back in that time, what was this, late 30s if you think about that recording what would you have — what would have been your entry point? What would you have focused on?

Wow. Normally I try to take some aspect of the recording and bring like a metaphor into it, okay? And then use that as a launch point for the review of the music itself. Okay? So let’s say for example “Body and Soul.” “Body and Soul” I believe was written by Johnny Green?
Yes. Heyman, Green, there are four names here.

Okay? So now I’m just doing a stream of consciousness, okay? Johnny Green went to Harvard, okay? He’s a very, very well educated person. Maybe there’s something there, all right, that can lead me into describing, at least initially, as an entree into this revolutionary recording. Okay? The other thing that I would also do is take somewhat of a comparative approach. Well there were other players of course, before. Historically what sort of influences might have been on Hawkins’ style, okay, who guided him in that direction, that influenced him on this particular recording and his other recordings. So you know it’s a hard thing to do right now, it’s almost like what we said before about is jazz dead. Because there’s been so much written about it, so we would have to go back in the H.G. Wells’ time machine back to that recording and listen to it with virgin ears. Okay? But again, like I said to you before, I try to take a methodical approach to it and believe me there’s lots of dead ends. There’s lots of dead ends. But the focus there, and here are some other angles that I might be interested in: What is the interaction of the rhythm section with such a revolutionary approach to improv? Okay? Here’s Hawkins really embellishing and playing and you know right from the get-go of his solo, well how is that interacting with the other players who may or may not be at a — while they are great players they may not be at a level of exploration that Hawkins was.

So it’s a really, really hard — you know that’s an interesting exercise in analysis. That’s a really, really, really good question and a really good exercise. And like anything else, sometimes you have to do exercises.
Yeah. If you can fit it into your schedule.
Well you know what? That’s a possibility. You know to look at it from virgin ears so to speak, and virgin eyes.
